lead: A chart is a survey, a date and a set of conventions. Learn to read all three and you know how far to trust it, on paper or on the plotter.

sections.title: The grid of a Mercator chart

qa.q: How do I measure distance in miles on a Mercator chart?
qa.a: On the **latitude scale** at the side of the chart, level with the leg: one minute of latitude is one mile. A minute of longitude is shorter, by the cosine of the latitude.

blocks.p: **Latitude** is read on the side scales, **longitude** at top and bottom, in minutes and decimals: 45 seconds is 0.75', not 0.45'. Count from the nearest printed line; west longitude grows leftward.

On a **Mercator** chart a straight line is a rhumb line: one true course throughout. Measure miles on the latitude scale level with the leg: a minute of latitude is a mile. A minute of longitude is shorter, by the cosine of the latitude: half a mile at 60°N.

At 1:200,000 a millimetre of pencil is 200 m. Plan on the passage chart, then change to the largest **scale** for each harbour; an inset has its own. On a measured distance, average the two runs' speeds, not their times.

qa.q: Why is my GPS position about 100 m out on an older paper chart?
qa.a: The chart is on an older **horizontal datum**, while GPS works in WGS84. Apply the shift printed in the title panel; with no shift given, carry the position across by bearing and distance from a charted object.

blocks.p: The **title panel** gives the scale, the units (a fathom is 1.83 m), the levels depths and heights are measured from, and the **horizontal datum**. GPS works in WGS84: on an older datum apply the printed shift, or the plot can be 100 m out. With no shift given, carry a position across by bearing and distance from a charted object.
The **compass rose** has an outer ring in true and an inner one in magnetic for the year printed. Update the variation and take it from the nearest rose.
The source diagram dates each survey: old lead-line work missed rocks. In a charted **magnetic anomaly** fix without the compass.

sections.title: Below datum, above datum, above high water

qa.q: What does an underlined number on a chart mean?
qa.a: It is a **drying height**, measured above chart datum. A plain sounding is a depth below chart datum, to which you add the height of tide; a figure in brackets is a height above MHWS that never covers.

blocks.p: A sounding is a depth below **chart datum**: add the height of tide. An underlined figure is a **drying height**, above datum. A figure in brackets is a height that never covers, measured above high water (MHWS).

blocks.p: Clearances are measured above HAT, or MHWS on older charts. A rock awash at datum shows only near low water. Keep outside the dotted danger line round a wreck or obstruction. A blank inside a contour is unsurveyed, not deep, and swell breaks on a shoal the sums allow.

sections.title: The seabed, the areas and their notes

qa.q: What do S, M and R next to a sounding mean when choosing where to anchor?
qa.a: They give the **nature of the seabed**: S sand, M mud and Cy clay are good holding; R rock, St stones, Wd weed and Sh shells are poor. Never anchor over a cable, pipeline or foul ground.

blocks.p: Never anchor over a cable, pipeline or foul ground. A **spoil ground** may be shallower than charted. **Overfalls** break at springs with wind against stream. A danger area may be firing: ask range control. In a prohibited area or reserve the chart's note decides; use the visitors' moorings. The tinted band between traffic lanes is the separation zone. Chart 5011 explains every symbol.

sections.title: The legend beside a light

qa.q: What does Fl(3) WR 15s 21m 18/15M mean beside a light on the chart?
qa.a: Three flashes every 15 seconds, with white and red **sectors**, 21 m above MHWS, nominal range 18 miles for the white and 15 for the red. The legend always runs character, colour, period, elevation, range.

refs: Chart symbols — AIS aids to navigation

blocks.p: The legend runs: character, colour, period, elevation, range. **Fl(3) WR 15s 21m 18/15M** is three flashes every 15 seconds, white and red sectors, 21 m above MHWS, nominal range 18 miles for white, 15 for red.

You see a light at its nominal range or its horizon, whichever is less: a 3M pierhead light will not show at 12 miles. **Sector** limits and obscured arcs are true bearings from seaward. Horn(2) 30s is two blasts every 30 seconds; a buoy's bell needs waves and may be silent in a calm. **Racon (T)** paints a Morse T on the radar beyond the mark. A virtual AIS mark exists only on screen.

sections.title: The newest information wins

qa.q: How do I correct a paper chart with Notices to Mariners?
qa.a: Find the last notice number in the chart's bottom-left margin, then apply every later **Notice to Mariners** for that chart in ink and write its number in the margin; temporary notices go in pencil.

refs: Charts — corrections and Notices to Mariners

blocks.p: **Notices to Mariners** carry the changes: a new breakwater, a moved buoy, a wreck. Each names the previous notice for that chart, so a gap shows. A new edition holds everything issued before its date.

Temporary notices: pencil, rubbed out later

blocks.p: Carry paper charts of the route and every likely port. Read the port page before arriving: whom to call, opening hours, water over the sill. When sources disagree, the newer wins: a corrected chart over an old pilot book, a fresh warning over the chart.

sections.title: The same data, with traps of its own

qa.q: What should I set the safety contour to on my chart plotter?
qa.a: To your draft plus a margin, along with the depth alarm. If the chart has no **safety contour** at that value, the plotter takes the next deeper one, and its route check ignores the tide.

blocks.p: A **raster** chart is a picture of the paper chart. A **vector** chart is a database: tap an object for its details, switch to night colours. It hides detail when zoomed out, so check each leg zoomed in; over-zooming enlarges errors, not accuracy.

Set the **safety contour** and depth alarm to draft plus a margin; with no contour at that value the plotter takes the next deeper one. Its route check ignores the tide: do that sum yourself. Mark a paper position every hour, so a dead plotter costs one hour of dead reckoning.
